story_text.value:
I built this because notifications never worked on me. I'd dismiss the alert and keep typing until my wrists hurt.

Pomlock is a Linux Pomodoro timer that locks your keyboard and mouse through evdev when your break starts, and covers the screen with a countdown overlay. You can't dismiss it until the break is over or keep working.

The whole thing runs as a terminal UI built with Textual. The home screen shows widgets for your session history, a chart of the week's stats, and progress against per-activity goals, all live while you work.

A few other things worth knowing: - `--no-block-input` if you want the timer without the hard lock - Custom work/break/long-break cycles, not just 25/5 (through the `-t` or `--timer` flags) - Tag sessions by activity and set daily/weekly/monthly goals per activity - Writes live state to a JSON file every second, so it plugs into Waybar or Polybar - You can pass a callback script (`--callback`) that runs on every phase change, I use mine to start focus music automatically

Install with `pipx install pomlock` or `uv tool install pomlock`.

Curious if anyone else has tried the "remove the choice" approach to breaks versus gentle reminders.

title.value: Show HN: Pomlock – Pomodoro timer that locks your keyboard until your break ends

story_text.value:
I got annoyed years ago that the Apple experience in Europe wasn’t the same as in the US (e.g. missing services or hardware differenceslike the US iPhone trading its SIM tray for a slightly larger battery).

With Apple Intelligence, the recent EU regulatory changes, and increasingly strange-looking hardware price differences, I realized I no longer had a clear picture of what was actually different.

So I built The Other Apple to put all of those differences in one place. Would love feedback on anything I’ve missed or gotten wrong.

story_text.value:
I've long been an index-investing type of person, but last year I started making some side bets, especially in tech (some inspired by WSB). I was sharing them with friends and wanted to simplify that.

This is how Investment Bets came about: you pick a ticker, a direction (long or short) and optionally a target date. The server fetches and records your entry price when you open the bet, and your exit price when you close it or reach the target date.

Each bet is scored on percentage gain/loss and has equal weight, so account size doesn't matter. The leaderboard sums your percentage results. I wanted to reward being right consistently, and since there's no compounding, a bad streak doesn't make your next good bets count for less.

The API is also open to AI agents. There's an OpenAPI file, llms.txt, Agent Skills under /.well-known and a single-file demo agent that reads headlines and places at most one bet per run. The checks that matter are in code (duplicate ticker, past target date, ticker the server can't resolve), so they don't depend on the model following the prompt. Agents get the same server-recorded prices as everyone else and show up on the same leaderboard.

https://investment-bets.com

https://investment-bets.com/agent

Please let me know if you have questions or feedback!

story_text.value:
Hi. I'm a self-employed dev of ~15 years mainly known for my SQLPro products. Recently my kids have been getting into drawing and I wanted a game like the old DrawSomething which I used to play a ton. It no longer seems to exist, and the alternatives I tried either had 'watch this ad' or 'pay for coins' to unlock either tools or drawing colours.

HankyDoodle is a draw-and-guess game for iOS and Android. The main part I enjoyed working on was the file storage. I had to come up with a format for the drawing animations that had to be small but store enough information to be able to animate it at playback speeds. It also had to be practical to store and serve hundreds of thousands of them - right now I'm sitting at slightly less than 20,000 drawings. Currently, the drawing sizes are typically between 1 and 12kb.

Drawings are recorded as a stream of operations that include each stroke's tool, colour, points and timing. The format (a small RLE/palette/varint container) and the renderer are one C core, which gets shared + linked multiple ways. This makes sure the rendering is byte-identical across all platforms (iOS, Android and WebAssembly). Unfortunately I did mess up some of the code used for flood fills and if I don't render the image at the same size the drawings come out slightly differently (for that reason I render all drawings at one size then resize after when I need thumbnails). Luckily I did build a version system into the drawings, so it's something future me (sucker) can deal with at some point.

Drawings are stored in S3 and served via CloudFront. The backend is PHP and MySQL, but built in a way that I should be able to scale it out/replace it as needed.

Although it was not originally planned, it makes a pretty neat demo that you can navigate to the website and playback drawings as well. https://hankydoodle.app/d/01M37AKQF6MCRRXCHB3YSAVBVG is an example of one of the more detailed drawings by someone with way more talent than me. The app has a 'word of the day' feature where users can submit their own artwork and that's an example of an extremely detailed one.

Features of the game:

- 1v1 async drawing and guessing. You draw a picture. Your opponent guesses when they get the chance.

- A forever guess mode. If you don't want to draw you can just go in and guess drawings made by others. Drawings get 'released' into the forever guess pool once a user has guessed the drawing.

- A word of the day where anyone can take a crack at drawing the word.

- A showcase where the best drawings can be found.

- Offline drawing, where you can draw while offline and without any sort of signup.

- A 'doodlepedia' where you can try and draw every word.

- An online portfolio of your drawings (such as https://hankydoodle.app/u/TP1N34).

- Privacy mode, where your drawings are private and only the folks you draw with can see them.

- Family mode where certain drawings and words get filtered completely out of your view.

The app has an unobtrusive banner ad which can be removed via a $3.99USD/year subscription. I know people don't like subscriptions, but that was the best alternative I could come up with and still keep the app free to most while covering my costs.

Happy to go deep on the format, the renderer, the fill, or the solo-dev tradeoffs.

story_text.value:
Howdy HN! I'm Charles and I wanted to share something I am working on right now: gangway (https://gangway.sh/).

Gangway is a simple way to quickly spin up ephemeral containers for previews, demos, artifacts, and temporary sharing

This app has started months ago as an idea to take advantage of spare compute capacity I have and to keep some of my hosting costs down. Initially I tried PaaS apps such as Coolify and Dokku, but it didn't provide a way for me to quickly and easily distribute apps I write by hand. Then, I tried creating a few prototypes and failing due to them being overly complex or broad scoped.

What I landed on was built one feature at a time:

- PR previews - This provided immediate utility to me for my frontend work. I get to review my teams code without being woried about usage or billing

- UI to quickly spin up a preview environment - If I have something I want to show a client but it isn't ready to go live on their domain yet, I can drag in a folder, let gangway figure out how to run it, optionally protect it with a password then send them a personalized URL.

- MCP - I thought it would be even easier if I can have an LLM deploy the app at any time without much thought. I have used this to message and quickly remedy and preview a bug fix from my phone before it shipped out.

- Artifacts - After adding the MCP I realized I often wanted my agent to generate visualizations or previews of features before implementation. Claude users may recognize the general idea from Artifacts, except these can be full stack apps you control.

Some examples currently running on gangway, all created from short conversations with different agents:

- Paged at 2 am - a user flow for a web-app on a canvas: https://paged-at-2am.demo.gangway.sh

- A slide deck from one markdown file (an artifact): https://four-day-week.demo.gangway.sh

- Bottle Sea, a small Bun + Postgres app: https://bottle-sea.demo.gangway.sh

- Quickfire Trivia - multiplayer rooms: https://quickfire-trivia.demo.gangway.sh

- A black hole: https://event-horizon.demo.gangway.sh

- FLUX a multiplayer physics demo: https://flux.demo.gangway.sh

Install is a one-liner or a quick docker compose setup (https://github.com/charlesabarnes/gangway#quickstart), and there's a local-only mode with cloudflare quick tunnel links if you don't want to expose anything.

I am considering deploying a multi-tenant hosted version of this to make it even easier. Let me know of any feedback that you may have!

story_text.value:
I’ve been building NetWasm: an independent .NET compiler, CoreLib and runtime designed specifically for WebAssembly. It compiles Roslyn-generated CIL into standalone core WASM or WASI Preview 2 components - without shipping CoreCLR or Mono.

A clean Release application containing Console.WriteLine(42) produces 82.5 KB of final WASM with WASI p2, including the runtime and precise garbage collector.

Website: https://www.netwasm.com/ Playground: https://playground.netwasm.com/

The playground runs fully on the browser without a backend / cloud server compiling your code - it's all WASM! Locally, you use dotnet new, dotnet build, dotnet test, etc like you would normally. You can run the self-contained .wasm output with wasmtime, fully portable.

GitHub repos: https://github.com/zion-sati/NetWasm https://github.com/zion-sati/NetWasm.Libraries

What is it?

It's CIL (used to be called MSIL - it's the dotnet bytecode in other words) to WASM compiler. But more than that it's intentionally not using Microsoft's Corelib. We avoid reflection, typename with full namespace strings etc where the resulting .wasm can end up bloated. The goal is to have C# (and later .NET in general - thus F# and VB.NET) be on equal footing as Kotlin/WASM. Note that Kotlin/WASM uses WasmGC, NetWasm uses BoehmGC in precise mode. NetWasm makes Wasm a first class target.

Why NetWasm?

I fell in love with C# in 2006 and have OSS attempts at building C#-like syntax using C++ template metaprogramming with BoehmGC a long time ago because I didn't like the idea of having a runtime pre-installed. This idea was revitalized when I tried to migrate my web UI framework FUI-RS to C# - the resulting smoke test was already a minimum of 1 MB Brotli compressed running in interpreter mode! FUI-RS (Rust) had it at under 50 KB uncompressed. What already works?

C# 15, precise GC, finalization, exceptions, generics, virtual/interface dispatch, LINQ, tasks / value tasks (thus async-await), JSON, dependency injection, regex, XML, HTTP, WIT/WASI and TUnit (a modern source generated unit testing framework) etc.

What's left to do?

There's a roadmap to v1.0 on the repo's README - tl;dr there's a lot to do before we can get there, e.g. Expression trees, faster dev loops, threading, web workers, interop via libimport and globalization (opt-in just like NetWasm's implementation of timezone info).

NuGet packages should be able to multitarget to support NetWasm as well as the full .NET as long as there's no reflection / typename involved.

Licence: Runtime, CoreLib, templates and libraries: MIT Compiler and tooling: NetWasm Community License

Note that NetWasm is pre-1.0 (currently v0.5) and evolving rapidly, so I'd appreciate any technical feedbacks from the community if you'd like to help me shape this project. Particularly, real WASI use cases people want supported, NuGet packages to multitarget (or even better if you're one of the popular open source packages and would like to start multitargeting).

Hi HN

I'm sharing a small (but hopefully fun!) sideproject I've been working on for the last few months.

I'm a big fan of daily games like Wordle, Connections, the Worldle etc... and have been wanting to make something similar for a while.

The idea kind of spun out of control and I ended up with a small platform for daily games. It currently has 10 games (+ 1 new game being tested))

This first iteration was more about building the platform and methodology for allowing me to add new games quickly and easily, so some of the games are pretty simple. I'm planning to add at least one new game per month from here on out. The games are available from the landing page without an account, but the full experience with an account is more fun with daily streaks, unlockables, and a leaderboard.

I would love some feedback on the idea, the site and the games. And if you have any ideas/suggestions for new games I would love to hear them.

story_text.value:
I have been working on search systems for a while, and I always wondered: What if search, instead of matching documents, matched workflows and ran those workflows?

I called it “Search that executes” — as opposed to search that retrieves information.

When AI agents showed up a few years ago, I realized that those workflows could be agents — capable of understanding a user’s query and taking branches dynamically. That’s when I got excited enough about the idea to implement it.

To make this work, it needs more than just search: a structured framework for defining agents (so the system “understands”), a controlled runtime for executing them with guardrails, and an end-to-end system with a UI to request and receive user approval before taking critical actions.

It made sense that all this plumbing should be handled behind the scenes, letting programmers concentrate on the agent’s business logic. Many design decisions followed directly from that.

Agents are created in a JSON structure. There are 23 “commands” that define the units of work an agent performs. Python expressions can be used in strings within curly braces.

Because the whole thing has a structure/schema, AI generates valid agents from English descriptions: “Create a RAG agent to call the company purchase order system”, “Create a tool-calling agent to …”. You can check this out in the live demo on the website.

The developer creates an agent, describes it in plain English, and publishes it in the system. Users just submit a request. Search matches the request to an agent, and the system runs the agent. The demo also shows searching for and executing agents.

That’s the central idea. The website has more information on other aspects. Despite the enterprise-y look and feel of the website, the system was really created by just me over the last couple of years. I would love to answer any questions and hear your comments and feedback.

story_text.value:
Hi folks!

Because of AI, there is more code to review. I don't know about you, but I get annoyed when the default git diff doesn't match something "obvious". I built CodeDiff to help.

It's a syntax-aware, careful implementation in Rust of all current research in code diffing. It parses 24 languages with TreeSitter and falls back to a modified Myers line diffing algorithm for any file it cannot parse. I wouldn't necessarily call it a novel algorithm, but it isn't a re-implementation of existing tools either.

I tested it on the last 50 commits of all 7400-or-so repositories that are in the Gentoo package list. CodeDiff can diff 99.95% of those file pairs in 120s and 6GB of RAM on a rusty 11 year old Intel E3-1275 v5. The median speed is 7ms and 93% of files are diffed in under 100ms.

I also did a bit of hand solving and have a test dataset of 1400 hand solved diffs. CodeDiff is perfect on 70% and near-perfect on 90% of them. But accuracy is actually a complex thing to measure, because if you are only after the AST diff, then it is perfect 89% of the time. Deciding what to paint however is not an objective thing so if you do try it out, check out the render options (press M) and make it fit your style.

If you just want to see how it looks like: https://ivankovic.github.io/codediff/showcase/?case=python-r...

If you want to install it: https://github.com/ivankovic/codediff

Do feel free to file issues. It's v0.1.1 at the moment, but I have been using it for months as my git difftool and I plan to keep that stable. Using it as a library directly from Rust however, might change until v1.0. The final goal for v1.0 is p99 < 400ms and 99% perfect diff, including multi-file diff support in 30 languages.

Credit where credit is due: There is a bunch of people researching diffs in the past 20 or so years. Without those papers, CodeDiff would be a lot harder to build. Especially without APTED and Myers algorithms.

License: AGPL3.0, I kind of like copy-left. If your company prevents use of AGPL software tell them to throw a few bucks my way for my token usage and we can talk.

AI disclosure: I use AI assisted coding. Claude and Mistral were used, heavily.
